description: Dawud and the Zabur, Maryam and the birth of Isa, the life and ascension of Isa, and Muhammad's preaching.
content_html:
The Prophet Dawud (David)

Dawud is one of the great prophet-kings of Islam. His story begins in Surah 2:249–251, where the young Dawud fights in the army of Saul (Talut in the Qur’an) against Goliath (Jalut). The narrative closely parallels 1 Samuel 17 but with theological emphasis: Dawud’s victory is not a result of his personal courage but of Allah’s power working through him. The verse states: “So they routed them by Allah’s leave, and Dawud killed Jalut; and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom.” Victory belongs to Allah; the role of the warrior is to be a willing instrument.

Dawud is also famous as a craftsman: he made armour. The Qur’an mentions this as a divine gift — Allah taught him to make coats of mail. This detail connects practical skill and craftsmanship to prophethood, showing that the prophets were fully engaged in the world rather than withdrawn from it.

Dawud is the author of the Zabur. Surah 17:55 affirms: “And We gave the Psalms to Dawud.” Muslims regard the Zabur as a genuine earlier revelation from Allah, alongside the Tawrat (Torah revealed to Moses) and the Injil (Gospel revealed to Isa). All three earlier scriptures are regarded as authentic in their original form, though Muslims believe they have been altered or corrupted over time, which is why the Qur’an was sent as the final, preserved revelation.

Maryam and the Birth of Isa

Maryam holds a unique position in Islam. She is the only woman mentioned by name in the Qur’an. An entire surah — Surah 19, which bears her name — is devoted to her story. This alone indicates her exceptional status: she is honoured as among the greatest women of all time and as a model of purity, devotion and submission to Allah.

Surah 19 describes the annunciation. The angel Jibril (Gabriel) appears to Maryam in the form of a man. He tells her Allah will give her a pure son. She asks: “How shall I have a son when no man has touched me, and I have not been unchaste?” Jibril replies: “So it will be. Your Lord says: It is easy for Me. And We will make him a sign to the people.” Isa is born miraculously, without a human father, by Allah’s direct creative command.

When Maryam presents the newborn Isa to her people, they accuse her of immorality. The infant Isa speaks from the cradle — a miracle unique to Islamic and certain apocryphal Christian traditions — declaring: “I am indeed a servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet.” This declaration is significant: even as a newborn, Isa affirms his status as a servant and prophet of Allah, not divine.

From a Humanist or atheist perspective, visions such as the visitation of Jibril to Maryam are not real supernatural events and provide no proof that Allah exists. They might argue that angelic visitations are a common feature of ancient religious narratives and reflect the way pre-scientific cultures explained unusual births or the founding of religious movements. A naturalistic reading would explain Maryam’s experience as a vision, a dream, or a later legendary development in the tradition.

Muslims respond that the annunciation is attested in both the Qur’an and the earlier Christian scriptures (the Gospel of Luke), giving it corroboration across revelation traditions. For Muslims, the miracle of Isa’s birth is a sign (ayah) of Allah’s power — just as he created Adam from dust with no father and no mother, he created Isa from Maryam with no father. Both are signs of the same creative power that sustains the universe.

The Prophet Isa: Life, Mission and Ascension

Isa is one of the five greatest prophets in Islam (the Ulu l-Azm, or prophets of firm resolve). He performed miracles: healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, and breathing life into clay birds. He received the Injil (Gospel) as a revelation from Allah. In Surah 61:6, Isa is recorded as foretelling: “And remember when Isa son of Maryam said: ‘O Children of Israel! I am Allah’s messenger to you, confirming the Torah before me and bringing good news of a messenger to come after me whose name shall be Ahmad.’” Muslims read “Ahmad” (another name for Muhammad) as Isa’s prophecy of the final prophet.

The most theologically significant passage about Isa is Surah 4:157–158, which deals with the manner of his death or departure from the world. The verse states: “And for their saying, ‘We have killed the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, the messenger of Allah’ — they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them. Those who disagree about it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except conjecture. They certainly did not kill him. Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself.”

This passage is the basis for the Islamic teaching that Isa was not crucified. Most Muslim scholars throughout history have interpreted the verse to mean that Allah raised Isa to himself before the crucifixion took place, and that someone else (or an illusion) was crucified in his place. This is a carefully held theological position — it does not deny that crucifixions happened in Roman Palestine, or that Jewish and Roman authorities sought to kill Jesus. It affirms that Allah protected his messenger from death in this way.

Key Fact

Surah 4:157–158 states that Isa “was not killed, nor was he crucified, but it was made to appear so.” Most Muslim scholars interpret this to mean Allah raised Isa before crucifixion occurred. This is an Islamic theological position — not a denial of history. Christians believe Isa (Jesus) died and rose; Muslims affirm he was raised to Allah without dying. This is the central Muslim–Christian divergence on Isa.

The Mission of Muhammad

The Prophet Muhammad received his first revelation in 610 CE in the cave of Hira near Makkah. Surah 26:213–217 records Allah’s command to Muhammad to begin preaching openly: “And warn your nearest kin.” This was the beginning of the public mission — Muhammad first approached his own clan and family, many of whom rejected him. The Qur’an records both the command to preach and the resistance he encountered.

Muhammad’s mission was to deliver the final and complete revelation from Allah, restoring the pure Tawhid that earlier prophets had taught but which human communities had corrupted. The Qur’an describes him as the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam al-Nabiyyin) — the last and final messenger, after whom no further prophet will come. His preaching met fierce opposition from the Quraysh tribe of Makkah, who had economic and social interests in maintaining the polytheistic religion of the Ka’ba.

The Islamic mission to call others to submission to Allah (Islam means “submission”) raises questions for non-religious thinkers about religious freedom and pluralism. Humanists would argue that in modern, pluralistic Britain, trying to convert other people to one’s religion shows a lack of respect for their autonomy and right to their own beliefs. They might also question the assumption that one religion possesses the final, complete truth.

Muslims respond that the Qur’anic command to preach is a command to invite and persuade — not to compel. Surah 2:256 states: “There is no compulsion in religion.” The model of Muhammad’s preaching in Makkah — enduring persecution for thirteen years before any military defence was permitted — shows that the Islamic approach to mission is fundamentally one of patient witness, not force. Divergent Muslim communities today interpret “calling to Islam” differently: some emphasise personal moral example; others engage in formal da’wah (invitation); others focus on social justice work as a form of witness.

Key Fact

In Surah 61:6, Isa foretells the coming of “a messenger after me whose name shall be Ahmad” — Muslims interpret Ahmad as another name of Muhammad. This places Isa in the prophetic chain that culminates in Muhammad, and frames the Injil (Gospel) as pointing forward to the final prophet. For Muslims, Christianity and Islam are not competing religions but successive stages of the same divine revelation.
exam_tip_html: The most sensitive exam question in this lesson concerns Surah 4:157–158. Always present it as an Islamic theological position, not as a historical claim: “In Islamic belief, the Qur’an teaches that Isa was not crucified but raised to Allah…” Do not phrase it as though you are adjudicating between Christianity and Islam. The 5-mark source question will likely ask about Isa or Maryam — cite the surah: “In Surah 19 (Maryam), Jibril announces the birth of Isa to Maryam…” For 12-mark Discuss questions, the non-religious argument (Humanist view on preaching, or visionary experiences not being proof of God) must be developed with genuine reasons, not just mentioned. SPaG: spell ‘Maryam’ (not Mary), ‘Jibril’ (not Gabriel) and ‘annunciation’ correctly in answers about the Qur’an.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dawud received the Zabur (Psalms) as revelation (Surah 17:55); his victory over Goliath (Surah 2:249–251) shows Allah’s power working through a willing human instrument.
  • Maryam (Surah 19) is the only woman named in the Qur’an; Jibril announced Isa’s miraculous birth; Surah 4:157–158 states Isa was not crucified but raised to Allah — the key Muslim–Christian divergence.
  • Isa foretold Muhammad in Surah 61:6; Muhammad received the command to preach in Surah 26:213–217; as the Seal of the Prophets, his mission completes and restores the chain of divine revelation.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about the Prophet Dawud.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Dawud defeated Goliath (Jalut) in battle by Allah's leave, and was given the kingdom and wisdom (Surah 2:249-251).
• Dawud was given the Zabur (Psalms) as a revelation from Allah (Surah 17:55).
• Allah taught Dawud to make armour — his craftsmanship is described as a divine gift.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Surah 19 (Maryam) says about the annunciation and birth of Isa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Jibril appeared to Maryam and announced that Allah would give her a pure son — she asked how this was possible since no man had touched her.
• Jibril replied 'Your Lord says it is easy for Me; We will make him a sign to the people.'
• When Maryam presented the newborn Isa to her people, he spoke from the cradle, declaring himself a servant and prophet of Allah.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Islamic teaching about Isa in Surah 4:157-158 differs from the Christian understanding.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• In Christianity, Jesus died on the cross and rose from the dead — the crucifixion is the central act of salvation. In Islam, Surah 4:157-158 states Isa was not killed or crucified; Allah raised him before death occurred — crucifixion is therefore not the basis of salvation in Islam.
• Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God who died to atone for human sin. In Islam, Isa is a great prophet and servant of Allah — born of a virgin, performing miracles — but not divine; his death (avoided by raising) is not understood as an atoning sacrifice.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Maryam is an important figure in Islam.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Maryam is the only woman named in the Qur'an and has an entire surah (Surah 19) named after her — this unique honour places her among the greatest figures in Islamic tradition, held up as a model of purity, faith and total submission to Allah's will.
• Maryam's experience of the annunciation and miraculous birth of Isa demonstrates Allah's unlimited creative power — 'Your Lord says it is easy for Me' (Surah 19) — and affirms that Allah can act outside natural processes when he chooses; this is a sign for believers.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 19 (Maryam) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'Muslims should not try to convert other people to Islam in modern Britain.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support (of the statement): Humanists argue that everyone has the right to their own beliefs and that attempting to convert others shows disrespect for religious freedom. In a pluralistic society, imposing one religion's truth claims risks division and harm. Non-Muslims may find attempts at conversion unwelcome or pressurising. Secular law in Britain protects freedom of religion.
Against: The Qur'an commands Muhammad to 'warn your nearest kin' (Surah 26:213-217) — a divine obligation that Muslims believe applies to all believers. Sharing one's faith is not the same as compulsion; Surah 2:256 states 'there is no compulsion in religion.' Da'wah (invitation) based on gentle persuasion and good example is the Islamic model, not force. Isa foretold Muhammad (Surah 61:6), showing that prophets always invited others — it is part of the prophetic tradition. Many Muslims see their commitment to social justice and ethical living as a form of witness that respects others' freedom.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things the Qur'an says about the life and mission of the Prophet Isa.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Isa was born miraculously of the virgin Maryam without a human father, by Allah's direct command.
• Isa performed miracles — healing the blind and leper, and raising the dead — as signs of his prophetic authority.
• Isa foretold the coming of a final messenger called Ahmad (Muhammad) in Surah 61:6.

knowledge_checks.q: Which surah is named after Maryam and tells the story of the annunciation?
What does Surah 4:157-158 teach about the fate of Isa?
options: He was crucified but not killed
He was not crucified; Allah raised him up

knowledge_checks.q: In Surah 17:55, Allah says 'We gave the Psalms (Zabur) to _____'.
Surah 61:6 records Isa foretelling the coming of a messenger called _____, whom Muslims identify as Muhammad.
Match each prophet to their key scripture or surah:
right: Surah 19 — the annunciation and birth of Isa

flashcard_questions.q: What did Allah give to Dawud according to Surah 17:55?
Where is Dawud's victory over Goliath (Jalut) described?

flashcard_questions.a: Mary — the only woman named in the Qur'an; her surah (Surah 19) tells the annunciation and birth of Isa.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 4:157-158 say about Isa's crucifixion?
flashcard_questions.a: He was not killed or crucified; it was made to appear so — Allah raised him to himself.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Isa foretell in Surah 61:6?
flashcard_questions.a: The coming of a messenger called Ahmad (another name for Muhammad).
The Gospel — the revelation given to Isa; Muslims believe it was authentic originally but has been partially corrupted.

flashcard_questions.q: What command did Allah give Muhammad in Surah 26:213-217?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Warn your nearest kin' — the beginning of his public preaching mission.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Seal of the Prophets' (Khatam al-Nabiyyin) mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Muhammad is the last and final prophet — no further prophet will come after him.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 2:256 say about religious conversion?
flashcard_questions.a: 'There is no compulsion in religion' — faith cannot be forced.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Maryam's status unique in the Qur'an?
flashcard_questions.a: She is the only woman named in the Qur'an and has an entire surah named after her.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three earlier divine scriptures that Muslims recognise alongside the Qur'an?
flashcard_questions.a: Tawrat (Torah — Musa), Zabur (Psalms — Dawud), Injil (Gospel — Isa).

glossary_terms.definition: The prophet known as David in the Bible; a warrior and king in Israel, author of the Zabur (Psalms), and messenger of Allah whose story is told across the Qur'an.
Protective metal garments; Dawud is described in the Qur'an as a maker of armour, which is mentioned as a divine gift.
The Psalms — the sacred scripture revealed to the Prophet Dawud; Muslims call it the Zabur and regard it as an authentic but now partially corrupted earlier revelation from Allah.
Mary, the mother of Isa (Jesus); the only woman mentioned by name in the Qur'an and the subject of an entire surah (Surah 19).
The announcement by the angel Jibril to Maryam that she would conceive and bear a son, Isa, by Allah's command — a divine miracle without a human father.
The archangel Gabriel in Islamic tradition; the angel who brought revelation to the Prophet Muhammad and who appeared to Maryam.
The prophet known as Jesus in Christianity; in Islam, Isa is one of the greatest prophets, born of a virgin, the Messiah, and raised to Allah without being crucified.
The Gospel revealed to the Prophet Isa; Muslims believe it was an authentic scripture from Allah, now partially corrupted in the Christian tradition.
The final prophet of Islam (c.570-632 CE); received the Qur'an as divine revelation and established the Muslim community.
